prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: EN · REST endpoints (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 5 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Endpoint" · longest unbreakable word 261px · one-line width 261px
  col 2: header "Method" · longest unbreakable word 55px · one-line width 55px
  col 3: header "Auth" · longest unbreakable word 46px · one-line width 46px
  col 4: header "Rate limit" · longest unbreakable word 57px · one-line width 68px
  col 5: header "Description" · longest unbreakable word 85px · one-line width 670px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"good","why":"Endpoint identifiers stay on one line and the description reads in four comfortable lines, but the Rate limit header is squeezed into two lines, making the header row uneven, and the description column is a touch tight."},"B":{"grade":"good","why":"Same solid structure as A with a slightly wider description (row 4 fits an extra word), but the Rate limit header still breaks across two lines, which weakens the header band."},"C":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Balanced proportions: Endpoint intact, Rate limit on a single header line, description wide enough for four lines per row; short Method/Auth columns carry only modest dead space."},"D":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Width is concentrated in Endpoint while the description is the narrowest of the intact layouts, forcing five to six lines per row and visibly taller rows; the imbalance hurts scanning."},"E":{"grade":"bad","why":"The Endpoint column is far too narrow, splitting unbreakable path identifiers mid-token ('/api/v1/session s', '/{jobId}/downlo ad'), and the description is also cramped—identifiers must never break."},"F":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Cleanest overall: one-line Rate limit header, endpoints intact, description wide enough for four balanced lines, and a calm rhythm across the narrow Method/Auth/Rate columns."}},"best":["F","C"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"Exact pixel widths of A/B/C/F are hard to distinguish visually and differ only marginally; whether the two-line 'Rate limit' header in A/B is a deliberate trade-off or just a side effect of width allocation is unclear."}
